tldr: This research models trajectories as discrete token sequences. By replacing tokens based on geometric collision information, it achieves both drastic route restructuring free from local minima and fast trajectory generation.
hero_caption: The overall concept of MGMP. Conventional continuous-space diffusion models and local optimization cannot escape dead ends (local minima). In contrast, MGMP combines discrete token representations with Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) to achieve jumps to alternative routes (structural repair) in one go.
overview:
In motion planning where robots avoid obstacles to reach a goal, approaches using deep generative models to produce diverse motion candidates have gained significant attention. However, conventional diffusion models denoise step by step in continuous space, which is computationally expensive. Furthermore, if a generated trajectory collides with obstacles, repairing it with local gradient-based methods leads to a fundamental weakness: getting trapped in local minima like dead ends, unable to escape to an alternative route.

Therefore, the authors thought: "What if we treat trajectories as coarse discrete tokens and boldly replace the collision-causing tokens with alternative candidates to jump directly to a different route?" To realize this, they proposed "MGMP," a new framework combining masked generative models with geometric guidance. A VQ-VAE discretizes trajectories into tokens, and a Masked Generative Transformer (MGT) generates initial trajectories in parallel at high speed. When a collision occurs, Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) intelligently narrows down and evaluates "where to re-mask and what alternative motion tokens to fill in" based on geometric information.

In validation experiments, the authors evaluated on challenging benchmarks such as "Ring Maze," where escaping dead ends is essential, and a "Controlled Route Invalidation" task that deliberately blocks the initial route. As a result, MGMP demonstrated overwhelming performance, outperforming the strongest baselines by more than 20 percentage points in success rate. Furthermore, it successfully generalized to unseen obstacle layouts, additional obstacles, unseen 3D mesh geometries, dual-arm coordinated robots, and real Baxter tasks, significantly advancing the practicality of generative motion planning.
contributions: Proposed "MGMP," a framework extending learned trajectory priors from "initial generation" to test-time "structural route repair."
Developed "Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS)," which efficiently identifies edit locations and filters candidate tokens using geometric gradients.
Constructed and released new benchmarks, "Ring Maze" and "Controlled Route Invalidation," to rigorously evaluate performance in escaping local minima.
Demonstrated high generalization and execution performance on unseen obstacle layouts, additional obstacles, unseen 3D mesh geometries, a dual-arm 14-DoF robot, and a real Baxter robot.

sections.heading: Why is continuous deformation alone not enough?
sections.summary: Many generative motion planners rely on continuous local optimization for test-time trajectory repair, failing to escape deep dead ends. MGMP addresses this problem by viewing trajectories as discrete tokens and reframing test-time repair as a "discrete search over prior-supported alternative motions."
sections.details:
Motion planning is the problem of finding a trajectory that moves a robot from a start pose to a goal pose while satisfying geometric constraints. Recently, methods that learn multi-modal trajectory distributions using deep generative models have flourished, but they have faced two major challenges.

The first is the "computational cost of initial trajectory generation." Diffusion models repeatedly denoise in high-dimensional continuous spaces, making them too heavy for real-time planning. The second is "test-time geometric repair." When a generated trajectory interferes with obstacles, it is typically repaired using gradient-based continuous trajectory optimization. However, if the initial trajectory falls into a dead end like a C-shaped obstacle, local deformation cannot pass through walls and cannot discover a completely different route.

Therefore, the authors asked: "Can we use the learned motion prior to jump to qualitatively different alternative routes and repair from the start?" This is the inspiration behind MGMP (Masked Generative Motion Planning).

In MGMP, trajectories are encoded into discrete token sequences beforehand. During initial generation, a Transformer predicts all tokens in parallel in a single forward pass, making it extremely fast. When a collision occurs, a mechanism called "Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS)" comes into play. From geometric information, it pinpoints "where to edit" (which tokens cause the collision) and efficiently searches "what to fill" (which alternative motions to use) from the Transformer's prior distribution. This enables structural repair involving global route restructuring, going beyond local fine-tuning.

captions.F1: The fundamental concept of MGMP. (a) In conventional continuous-space approaches, local optimization gets trapped in potential valleys and cannot overcome dead ends. (b) In MGMP, replacing discrete tokens allows an instant jump to another energy valley, enabling dramatic route restructuring.

sections.heading: From classical methods to generative models, and on to masked discrete representations
sections.summary: This section reviews classical sampling-based methods, trajectory optimization, and recent diffusion-based planners, summarizing their respective weaknesses. MGMP's uniqueness lies in fusing masked generative models with robotic geometric repair for the first time.
sections.details:
This section organizes related work into three lines of research:

### Classical and Learning-Based Motion Planning
Sampling-based methods like RRT* can explore broad spaces to discover alternative routes, but in high-dimensional spaces or intricate environments, they require an enormous number of collision checks, causing computation time to explode. Meanwhile, trajectory optimization methods such as CHOMP and TrajOpt produce smooth trajectories quickly, but they are highly sensitive to initialization and easily trapped in local minima. To overcome these, diffusion models that learn trajectory distributions (such as MPD and PBD) have emerged, but as long as they rely on continuous optimization for test-time repair, escaping deep local minima remains difficult.

### Discrete Representations and Masked Generative Models
Recently, research on compressing motions and trajectories into discrete latent representations (tokens) has advanced. In particular, Masked Generative Transformers treat images as multiple discrete tokens, achieving fast and high-quality generation through parallel generation and iterative mask re-prediction. This paper takes a novel approach by extending this masked generative paradigm to robot motion planning with collision constraints.

### Test-Time Trajectory Modification and Repair
Existing methods for modifying generated trajectories at test time have mainly focused on continuous gradient guidance or fixed token searches. However, these were aimed at general generation quality improvement or were computationally heavy, unable to target and repair robot-specific geometric constraint violations directly. MGMP sets itself apart from existing work by leveraging the learned motion prior itself as a "geometry-guided search space."

sections.heading: The mechanism of geometry-guided token search
sections.summary: MGMP consists of a VQ-VAE that discretizes trajectories into tokens, an MGT that predicts tokens conditionally in parallel, and GGTS that identifies and replaces collision points using geometric gradients. It features a two-stage setup: switching global routes via coarse discrete search, followed by brief continuous optimization for polishing.
sections.details:
MGMP's core architecture and algorithm consist of the following three components:

### 3.1 Discretizing the Motion Space with a Codebook
First, to convert a continuous trajectory $x$ into a compact discrete token sequence $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_N)$, a 1D-CNN-based VQ-VAE (Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder) is trained. The encoder groups several timesteps of motion into a single token and quantizes it to the nearest vector in a learnable codebook $\mathcal{K}$. The decoder reconstructs a smooth continuous trajectory from this sequence of embedding vectors.

### 3.2 Motion Prediction with Masked Generative Transformer (MGT)
Next, a Masked Generative Transformer (MGT) is trained to predict trajectory tokens conditioned on the start pose $c_s$, goal pose $c_g$, and obstacle information $w$. During training, a portion of tokens is randomly masked (or corrupted), and a cross-entropy loss is used to reconstruct the original tokens. During inference, all tokens can be predicted in parallel in a single forward pass, eliminating the multi-step iterative computation required by diffusion models.

### 3.3 Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS)
Even when the MGT outputs a trajectory with high confidence, it may collide with obstacles after decoding. This is where GGTS comes in. It performs structural repair on the trajectory in two steps:

- **Where to edit**: Gradients of the collision evaluation function $J$ (such as a Signed Distance Function, SDF) are backpropagated to each token embedding through the decoder. By combining gradient magnitude with model confidence, a score $s_i$ is computed, adaptively "re-masking" top tokens that contribute most to the collision. For shallow collisions, only a few tokens are masked; for deep collisions, a broader range of tokens is masked.
- **What to fill**: For masked positions, top-$M$ candidate codes are proposed from the MGT prior. Since decoding and validating all candidates is computationally heavy, candidates are first screened to the top-$k$ promising ones using a first-order approximation score via Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. After that, they are actually decoded, and tokens are committed only if the exact geometric cost $J$ improves.

After repeating this discrete token replacement for several rounds to complete the global route change, a few steps of continuous gradient descent (Polishing) are applied as a finishing touch to remove minor interferences.

sections.heading: From escaping dead ends to dual-arm coordination and real-robot validation
sections.summary: In the "Ring Maze" benchmark evaluating escape from local minima and tasks forcibly invalidating initial trajectories, MGMP achieved success rates significantly outperforming baselines. It also demonstrated superior generalization and repair capability on unseen obstacle geometries, additional obstacles, a 14-DoF dual-arm system, and a real Baxter robot.
sections.details:
To verify the true value of MGMP, the authors designed a thorough experimental protocol.

### 4.1 Evaluating Escape from Local Minima
- **Ring Maze (C-shaped maze)**: A 2D environment densely packed with 7 C-shaped obstacles, where trajectories easily get trapped in local minima. MGMP achieved a 96% success rate (67% valid sample rate). In contrast, conventional trajectory optimization method CHOMP and diffusion-based PBD only reached valid sample rates in the 20% range. Remarkably, even "MGMP w/o Polish," which omits the finishing continuous optimization, recorded a 91% success rate, showing that GGTS alone manages to escape in almost all cases.
- **Controlled Route Invalidation (Kuka arm)**: An experiment purely comparing repair capability by providing all methods with the identical, pre-blocked initial trajectory. MGMP achieved an 82% repair success rate, overwhelming STOMP (57%) and continuous embedding optimization (60%). In successful trajectories, an average of 71.7% of all tokens were replaced, confirming a bold reorganization into a detour route rather than mere minor adjustments.

### 4.2 Generalization and Scalability to Unseen Environments
- **Unseen Layouts and High DoF**: In the 14-DoF DualKuka environment, MGMP achieved a 96% success rate with a planning time of 0.39 seconds, far surpassing BIT* (85%, 2.01 seconds) and PBD (79%).
- **Additional Obstacles and Unseen Meshes**: In environments with more obstacles than during training, or environments with unseen ShapeNet daily object meshes (cameras, guitars, etc.), combining with differentiable costs via DeepSDF maintained high success rates.

### 4.3 Ablations and Real-Robot Experiments
Ablation studies proved that both geometric gradients for edit localization and probability-based candidate screening are indispensable. Furthermore, on a real Baxter robot across shelf-placing, button-pressing, and pen-drawing tasks, generated trajectories executed flawlessly without failure in the real environment.

sections.heading: Making full use of generative priors as a "search tool"
sections.summary: MGMP demonstrated that learned trajectory priors can be utilized not just as "initial generators," but as "structural search spaces" linked with geometric information. The division of roles between global route restructuring via discrete token replacement and local continuous optimization provides a new guideline for future planning.
sections.details:
The biggest takeaway of this research is rethinking the conventional division of labor where one simply takes a generative model's output and passes it to continuous optimization.

By mapping trajectories into a discrete token space beforehand, ultra-fast 1-step parallel generation via a Transformer becomes possible at inference time. And when geometric failure occurs, rather than struggling in continuous space, the system conducts a top-down search within the same token space for "which motion blocks to replace to satisfy geometric constraints."

As the authors demonstrated, this hybrid division of labor—where discrete search (GGTS) handles the heavy lifting of global route restructuring and a few steps of continuous optimization (Polishing) handles only final minor interference removal—was the key to achieving overwhelming robustness and speed in high-dimensional, complex environments.

This mindset represents a powerful paradigm shift that can be broadly applied beyond robot motion planning to various generative tasks with geometric or physical constraints, such as manipulation or locomotion pattern adaptation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and further qualitative results
sections.summary: This appendix supplements self-collision avoidance for dual-arm robots, extension to numerous obstacles (a Product-of-Experts-style formulation), and architectural details of VQ-VAE and MGT. It also provides empirical data on why MGMP repairs reliably even under severe deep collisions.
sections.details:
The appendix provides important formulations and experimental results not fully covered in the main text.

### Extension to Multiple Obstacles and Dual-Arm Tasks
- **Considering Self-Collision**: For dual-arm robots, in addition to environmental interference, an arm-to-arm collision term is added to the objective function $J$ to backpropagate gradients.
- **Handling Numerous Obstacles**: When there are more obstacles than during training, the obstacle set is partitioned, individual prediction logits are computed, and they are summed together in an approach similar to "Product of Experts." This handles dense environments without retraining the model.

### Robustness to Collision Depth
The analysis in Appendix C.1 shows repair success rates according to how deeply initial trajectories penetrate obstacles (negative clearance values). Continuous guidance methods like PBD drop sharply to a 5.2% repair rate when penetration becomes deep (below $-0.15$), because local gradients cannot push the trajectory outside the obstacle. In contrast, MGMP maintained a high repair rate of 71.4% under the same severe conditions. This is because the entire collision region is boldly re-masked using geometric scores, proposing completely different intermediate tokens.

captions.F8: Qualitative comparison on the 7-DoF Kuka arm in an unseen obstacle layout. Comparing trajectories of BIT*, PBD, and MGMP, MGMP stably generates feasible trajectories weaving through crowded obstacles.

takeaways: Discretizing trajectories with VQ-VAE enables both ultra-fast parallel generation via Transformers and global route restructuring through token replacement.

In test-time trajectory repair, relying solely on continuous optimization cannot escape dead ends. A two-stage approach—switching global routes via discrete search and fine-tuning with continuous optimization—is extremely effective.
Geometric gradients are most critical for identifying collision locations, and combining them with model confidence enables lean, adaptive masking.
limitations: Because the method assumes geometric obstacle information such as SDFs (Signed Distance Functions) and differentiable cost computation, robustness to noisy point clouds obtained directly from sensors remains a topic for future verification.
Hyperparameter tuning in geometry-guided search, such as the number of search candidates and re-masking thresholds, may depend on task characteristics.
In real-robot experiments, simple fixed primitives (such as descending motions) were called after 3D spatial motions, and end-to-end dynamic control involving physical contact was not addressed.
